title: Exercise 4:  Estimate precision and uncertainty
text:
This series of exercises focuses on the precision of estimates calculated from Labour Force Survey data, in other words the degree to which we can trust them to reflect the likely values in the population. In order to do this, we will compute similar measures as before - means and proportions but this time we will be focusing on their confidence intervals.
Learning objectives:

title: Exercise 4:  Estimate precision and uncertainty
text:
Data
In this exercise we will be using Quarterly LFS data for October-December 2024.
To follow the exercise, you need to access the relevant dataset from the UK Data Service: Quarterly Labour Force Survey, October - December, 2024.

title: Exercise 4:  Estimate precision and uncertainty
section: 1. Weighted and unweighted confidence intervals of mean weekly earnings
text:
1. Weighted and unweighted confidence intervals of mean weekly earnings
In this exercise, we will be comparing the mean gross weekly earnings (GRSSWK) and their confidence intervals using weighted and unweighted estimates. As previously, we will be using the weighting variable specifically designed for earnings: PIWT24.
First, let’s examine gross weekly earnings and compute its unweighted mean:

*** Raw variable
summ GRSSWK

*** Removing non-responses
summ GRSSWK if GRSSWK>=0

quietly histogram   GRSSWK if GRSSWK>0, xtitle("Earnings (£)") title("Gross weekly earnings in the UK, Oct-Dec 2024")



    Variable |        Obs        Mean    Std. dev.       Min        Max
-------------+---------------------------------------------------------
      GRSSWK |     63,069    75.80171    316.4214         -9      23076


    Variable |        Obs        Mean    Std. dev.       Min        Max
-------------+---------------------------------------------------------
      GRSSWK |      7,210    732.4975    623.6522          5      23076




We can compute the mean this way:

mean GRSSWK if GRSSWK>=0


Mean estimation                          Number of obs = 7,210

--------------------------------------------------------------
             |       Mean   Std. err.     [95% conf. interval]
-------------+------------------------------------------------
      GRSSWK |   732.4975   7.344713      718.0997    746.8953
--------------------------------------------------------------


By default, Stata provides a ‘naive’ unweighted confidence interval of the mean. As a reminder, the 95% confidence interval of a mean is the value of the mean plus or minus 1.96 times its standard error. The standard error itself is the standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size.
We could now say - incorrectly - that on the basis of unweighted sample values, we are 95% confident that the overall mean of gross weekly earnings in the UK population range between £718 and £747 per week, that is an interval of about £29.
Let’s now compute the weighted mean and confidence interval of GRSSWK. There are different ways of doing this in Stata. We will be using the same survey data specific functions as in previous exercises.

*** Let's declare our data to be survey data with PIWT as weight. 
svyset [pw=PIWT24]
 
*** ... Then get the weighted mean 
svy:mean GRSSWK



Sampling weights: PIWT24
             VCE: linearized
     Single unit: missing
        Strata 1: <one>
 Sampling unit 1: <observations>
           FPC 1: <zero>

(running mean on estimation sample)

Survey: Mean estimation

Number of strata =      1         Number of obs   =     63,069
Number of PSUs   = 63,069         Population size = 29,332,807
                                  Design df       =     63,068

--------------------------------------------------------------
             |             Linearized
             |       Mean   std. err.     [95% conf. interval]
-------------+------------------------------------------------
      GRSSWK |   693.7501   6.073396      681.8463     705.654
--------------------------------------------------------------



QuestionsAnswers



What are the bounds between which we can be sure 95% of the values can be found, once we weight the data?
How wide is the weighted confidence interval?
What is the effect of weighting the data on the precision of estimates?




It is between £682 and £706 per week
£24
In general, confidence intervals and standard deviations of weighted estimates tend to be wider than those of unweighted estimates, which makes them at the same time more representative but less precise. However, the opposite is true here: the weighted confidence intervals of GRSSWK are narrower than the unweighted ones.

3. Adjusting CIs with published design effects
Design effects account for the impact of survey design (e.g., clustering and stratification) on the precision of estimates. Here, we will be adjusting the CI of the proportion of women and men employed (ILODEFR) in manufacturing (INDE07M) in their main job using design effects published in Volume 1 of the LFS documentation.
Let’s begin by examining the sector variable and creating dummy variables. We recode “Does not apply” as system missing but keep the non responses (-8).

ta INDE07M if INDE07M!=-9,gen(IndSect)

The above confidence intervals do not take into account the survey design and depending on the variable, maybe too narrow ie overstate the precision of the estimates - or too wide.
In order to compute more robust CIs or standard errors, we need to have access to survey design variables such as strata and primary sampling units identifiers. These are unfortunately withheld by the producers of the LFS due to concerns about potential risk of disclosure of personal information.
Another approach that can be implemented for some headline estimates consists in adapting confidence intervals based on the design factors (DEFF) published by the ONS. These can be found in the Volume 1 of the LFS documentation. For the October-December 2024 edition, this file is called: lfs_user_guide_vol1_background_2024.pdf.












The design effects for the proportion of females and males employed in manufacturing are respectively 1.2216 and 1.3048:












We now need to adapt these to the confidence intervals we computed earlier. In order to do this, we need to start with the standard errors - as the DEFF are meant to adjust these. We can then obtain the adjusted CIs for females.
From the above table, we can see that the proportion of women employed in manufacturing is 4.83, the standard error of this proportion, 0.19. From the documentation, we know that the design factor is 1.2216. We are now able to compute the adjusted confidence intervals for females by hand:

*** Lower bound
dis 4.82-1.96*sqrt(0.19*1.2216)

*** Upper  bound
dis 4.82+1.96*sqrt(0.19*1.2216)


3.8757274

5.7642726


… For males: the proportion employed in manufacturing is 11.01, the standard error 0.28 and the design factor is 1.3048:

*** Lower bound
dis 10.98-1.96*sqrt(0.27*1.3048)

*** Upper  bound
dis 10.98+1.96*sqrt(0.27*1.3048)


9.8166513

12.143349



QuestionsAnswers



What has happened to the confidence intervals after we adjusted them?
What if we wanted to adjust our earlier estimates of gross weekly earnings for the design effects?



1.They have widened, which means that in this case, not taking the survey design led us to overestimate the precision of estimates.
2. We would not be able to do this with the safeguarded version of the data as there are no design factors for earnings published by the ONS. We would need to use the secured version of the data, and compute the adjusted estimates ourselves using the appropriate survey functions.

title: Exercise 3: Labour Market Flows
text:
The exercise presents three different methods for examining labour market flows - ie the transitions between one kind of involvement in paid work (for example, full-time employed) to another one (for example, economically inactive) using longitudinal data from the Labour Force Survey.
The estimates in this exercise relate to figures published by ONS on the ‘Labour market flows NSA’ sheet in Table X02. NSA stands for ‘non seasonally adjusted’, as we will be examining flows that took place between two quarters (as opposed to seasonally adjusted yearly averages).
Learning outcomes:

The exercise presents three different methods for examining labour market flows - ie the transitions between one kind of involvement in paid work (for example, full-time employed) to another one (for example, economically inactive) using longitudinal data from the Labour Force Survey.

title: Exercise 4:  Estimate precision and uncertainty
text:
This series of exercises focuses on the precision of estimates produced from Labour Force Survey data—that is, how much the results might vary due to sampling. To explore this, we’ll calculate the same types of measures as before—means and proportions—but this time we’ll pay particular attention to their confidence intervals.
Learning objectives:

To be able to compute and interpret confidence intervals of earnings in the LFS;
To be able to assess the impact of weighting on weighting ;
To be able to interpret CIs for regional differences;
To be able to use published LFS design effects and apply them to your own estimates;



In this exercise we will be using Quarterly LFS data for October-December 2024.
To follow the exercise, you need to access the relevant dataset from the UK Data Service: Quarterly Labour Force Survey, October - December, 2024.



We suggest that you create a folder named LFS_exercises as the working directory for this exercise – where syntax files and other materials will be stored. After downloading the data, save it in an easily accessible location within LFS_exercises, such as a subfolder named Data.
First let’s load the packages that we are going to need:

library(haven)  ### Functions to open Stata or SPSS datasets
library(dplyr)  ### Easier data manipulation
library(survey) ### Survey data analysis functions
library(srvyr)  ### Easier  manipulation of survey data

Let’s open the dataset.

setwd ("LFS_exercises")

### Importing a Stata format dataset 
lfs_od24 <- read_dta(
        "Data/UKDA-9349-stata/stata/stata13/lfsp_od24_eul_pwt24.dta"
                    )

As there are many variables in the LFS, let’s create a data frame with just those required for this exercise. We also convert the original variables into factors in order to make them easier to work with.

dataex4 <- lfs_od24 |>
  select(PERSNO, PIWT24, PWT24,GRSSWK, INECAC05, ILODEFR,
         FTPT, HOURPAY, SEX,INDE07M,GOVTOF2 ) |>
  mutate(
         across(
         c(INECAC05:GOVTOF2),\(x) as_factor(x, "both")
               )
         ) |>
  droplevels()




In this exercise, we will be comparing the mean gross weekly earnings (GRSSWK) and their confidence intervals using weighted and unweighted estimates. As previously, we will be using the weighting variable specifically designed for earnings: PIWT24.
First, let’s examine gross weekly earnings and compute its unweighted mean:

### Raw variable
summary(dataex4$GRSSWK)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   -9.0    -9.0    -9.0    75.8    -9.0 23076.0 

### Removing non-responses

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
    5.0   413.2   615.0   732.5   923.0 23076.0 

### Plotting incomes up to the 99th percentile
hist(dataex4$GRSSWK[dataex4$GRSSWK>=0 & 
                    dataex4$GRSSWK<=quantile(dataex4$GRSSWK[dataex4$GRSSWK>=0],.99)],
     main= "Distribution  of weekly earnings, October-December 2024",
     xlab = "Gross Weekly Earnings (£) -- 1st-99th percentiles, Oct-Dec 2024")







### Computing the mean
mw<-mean(dataex4$GRSSWK[dataex4$GRSSWK>=0],na.rm=T)

mw

[1] 732.4975


Let’s now compute the confidence interval. We need to do it by hand, using the standard deviation.

s.mw<-sd(dataex4$GRSSWK[dataex4$GRSSWK>=0],na.rm=T)

s.mw

[1] 623.6522


As a reminder, the 95% confidence interval of a mean is the value of the mean plus or minus 1.96 times its standard error. The standard error itself is the standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size:

se<-s.mw/sqrt(nrow(dataex4[dataex4$GRSSWK>=0,]))

lb<-mw-(1.96*se)
ub<-mw+(1.96*se)

round(c(mw,lb,ub))

[1] 732 718 747


We could now say - incorrectly - that on the basis of unweighted sample values, we are 95% confident that the overall mean of gross weekly earnings in the UK population ranges between £718 and £747 per week, that is an interval of £29.
Let’s now look at the weighted estimates. We will be using the same survey data specific functions as in previous exercises.

### Let's declare our data to be survey data with PIWT as weight. 
dataex4.s<-as_survey_design(weights=PIWT24,dataex4)
 
### ... Then get the weighted mean
mw.s<-dataex4.s|>
      summarise(survey_mean(GRSSWK,vartype = "ci"))

mw.s

# A tibble: 1 × 3
   coef `_low` `_upp`
  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
1  694.   682.   706.

What are the bounds between which we can be sure 95% of the values can be found, once we weight the data?
How wide is the weighted confidence interval?
What is the effect of weighting the data on the precision of estimates?




It is between £682 and £706 per week
£24
In general, confidence intervals and standard deviations of weighted estimates tend to be wider than those of unweighted estimates, which makes them at the same time more representative but less precise. However, the opposite is true in this case: the weighted confidence intervals of GRSSWK are narrower than the unweighted ones.

title: Exercise 4:  Estimate precision and uncertainty
text:
Design effects account for the impact of survey design (e.g., clustering and stratification) on the precision of estimates. Here, we will be adjusting the CI of the proportion of women and men employed (ILODEFR) in manufacturing (INDE07M) in their main job using design effects published in Volume 1 of the LFS documentation.
Let’s begin by examining the sector variable:

cbind(Freq.=table(dataex4$INDE07M[dataex4$ILODEFR=="[1] In employment"]),
      Pct.=round(100*

      )

Let’s then compute the proportion of men and women employed in manufacturing. We leave out “Does not apply” as system missing but keep the non responses later.

fem<-dataex4.s |>  
   filter(SEX=="[2] Female" & 
          ILODEFR=="[1] In employment" &
          INDE07M!="[-9] Does not apply") |>

   filter(SEX=="[1] Male" &

The above confidence intervals do not take into account the survey design and depending on the variable, maybe too narrow ie overstate the precision of the estimates - or too wide.
In order to compute more robust CIs or standard errors, we need to have access to survey design variables such as strata and primary sampling units identifiers. These are unfortunately withheld by the producers of the LFS due to concerns about potential risk of disclosure of personal information.
Another approach that can be implemented for some headline estimates consists in adapting confidence intervals based on the design factors (DEFF) published by the ONS. These can be found in the Volume 1 of the LFS documentation. For the October-December 2024 edition, this file is called: lfs_user_guide_vol1_background_2024.pdf.

text:
In this exercise, we will recreate an ONS labour market estimate published online in the table EMP07 Temporary Employees. Currently, this table is updated four times a year in February, May, August and November using the Quarterly Labour Force Survey (QLFS).
Learning outcomes:

To become more familiar with QLFS datasets.
To become familiar with producing weighted population estimates
To understand how some ONS estimates are produced



The data used in this exercise relates to an estimate published by the ONS for October-December 2024.
To follow the exercise, you need to access the relevant dataset from the UK Data Service: Quarterly Labour Force Survey, October - December, 2024.



We suggest that you create a folder named LFS_exercises as the working directory for this exercise – where syntax files and other materials will be stored. After downloading the data, save it in an easily accessible location within LFS_exercises, such as a subfolder named Data.
First let’s load the packages that are are going to need…

title: Estimates of temporary employment
text:
In order to provide reliable estimates of population values, survey data needs to be weighted when analysed. Weights are variables whose values increase or decrease the relative importance of observations, depending on how likely respondents were to take part to the survey. Some weights are only designed to correct the relative importance of observations, whereas others in addition also enable calculating population totals - the latter are called grossing weights.
Below, we compare weighted and unweighted frequencies and percentages.
We will be using as_survey_design(), a R function from the survey and srvyr packages that in effect creates a weighted version of our data.
Let us first examine the variable measuring - JOBTYP - whether respondents work in a temporary job or not:

cbind("Freq"=table(dataex1$JOBTYP), 
      "Pct"=  100*prop.table(table(dataex1$JOBTYP)) |> round(1) 
      )

                               Freq Pct
[-9] Does not apply           36698  60
[-8] No answer                   15   0
[1] Permanent                 25104  40
[2] Not permanent in some way  1252   0


… and create a version without missing values.

dataex1 <- dataex1 |> 
          mutate (
                 JobTmp = ifelse(JOBTYP == "[2] Not permanent in some way",
                                 "Temporary",
                                  "Not temporary"),
                 JobTmp = ifelse(JOBTYP == "[-9] Does not apply" | 
                                  JOBTYP == "[-8] No answer",
                                  NA,
                                  JobTmp),
                 JobTmp = as.factor(JobTmp)
                  )

cbind("Freq"=table(dataex1$JobTmp), 
      "Pct"=  (100*prop.table(table(dataex1$JobTmp))) |> round(1) 
      )

               Freq  Pct
Not temporary 25104 95.2
Temporary      1252  4.8


We create a survey design - informed version of the data that we will be using for susbsequent analysis:

dataex1.s<-dataex1|> 
         filter(!is.na(PWT24) ) |> 
         as_survey_design(weights=PWT24)

Please note that we needed to remove observations with missing weights values, in effect observations that should not be taken into account to calculate population values. If we don’t we will get an error message.
We can now compute the weighted distribution of JobTmp:

t<-svytable(~JobTmp, dataex1.s)


cbind("Freq"=t, 
      "Pct"=  (100*prop.table(t)) |> round(1) 
      )

Not temporary 27802100 94.8
Temporary      1514206  5.2
